newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba defiant amid Spanish pressure for change.
newsitem.headline: Cuba defiant amid Spanish pressure for change.

text.p: Cuba, engaged in a diplomatic spat with Spain over calls from Madrid for political reform, insisted on Wednesday that it would not make changes under pressure from anyone.

An annual government-organized rally held every Nov. 27 to mark the death by firing squad of eight medical students under Spanish colonialism in the 19th century took on a particular significance this year amid the row with Madrid.

Senior officials including Vice President Carlos Lage and Foreign Minister Roberto Robaina attended the rally of thousands of students, which marched through the city from Havana University to a memorial near the Spanish Embassy.
The embassy itself was guarded by hundreds of police and members of civil order groups standing in lines to prevent people from getting near.
The streets immediately around the building were sealed off, apparently to avoid any incident involving the embassy.

Speaking at the rally, Victoria Velazquez, head of the Union of Young Communists, did not directly mention Spain as she told the crowd that Cuba was determined to stick with its system and stand by President Fidel Castro.
But her message was clear on a day when Cuba affirms its independence by marking the memory of the students, viewed as martyrs of the 19th century independence wars against Spain.
Velazquez told the crowd that there will be "no provocateurs or opportunists with the strength to break the tranquility and stability of this working people."
"Cuba is not afraid of anybody or anything," she said.
"The only change possible here is the revolution of Jan. 1, 1959," she said, referring to the day Castro took power.
Tensions have simmered for weeks between Havana and Madrid over a steady stream of criticism of Cuba's one-party communist system by Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar.
They boiled over on Tuesday when Cuba angrily accused the Spanish government of meddling in its internal affairs and withdrew its official approval for a new Spanish ambassador.

In Washington, the U.S. State Department praised Spain for criticizing human rights practices in Cuba. "We're obviously very pleased that a European leader is now standing up to defend human rights and democracy in Cuba," department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.

But amid the diplomatic spat, Cuba appeared keen to prevent any disturbances around the embassy, mounting the huge security operation and denying rumors among Cubans that Spain had changed its visa policy for Cubans.

The Foreign Ministry issued a statement on Wednesday saying that in response to a request from the Spanish Embassy it was informing the public that the Spanish consular service was operating normally.
Opening hours and procedures for visa requests and other embassy business remained the same, the statement said.
"The Ministry of Foreign Affairs adds that rumors that the granting of visas by this (Spanish) consulate in a more rapid or special way are totally false," the statement added.
Several hundred people gathered around the embassy building on Tuesday following news of Cuba's protest to Spain.

The crowds appeared to be partly people curious to see if anything was happening, and partly Cubans thinking that there might be an increased chance of obtaining a visa or seeking asylum in the embassy.
